question: What is the difference between VAULT_BUSY and ENTRY_CONFLICT -- when does each one fire, and why are they two separate mechanisms?
answer_hinglish: Dono errors concurrency races ko signal karte hain, lekin bilkul alag level par aur alag tareeke se. VAULT_BUSY VAULT-LEVEL claim se aata hai -- claimEntryOp() ya changeMasterPassword ke apne checks (record.rotating, record.pendingEntryOps) -- aur yeh BEFORE any real work reject karta hai: caller ne kuch kiya hi nahi, bas galat waqt par try kiya. Yeh ek entry-op aur ek rotation ke beech lagta hai, kabhi bhi do entry-ops ke beech nahi (woh dono allowed hote hain, independent ids par ya version check se). ENTRY_CONFLICT ENTRY-LEVEL hai -- yeh tab aata hai jab DO ALREADY-IN-FLIGHT updates (ya update-vs-delete) ne apna kaam poora kar liya (apna commit bhi successfully kar diya), aur commit ke baad pata chala ki SAME entry par koi aur pehle jeet gaya. Dono operations ne store tak apna write bheja, lekin version mismatch loser ko pakadta hai. Matlab VAULT_BUSY 'tumne try hi nahi kiya, kyunki rotation chal rahi thi' hai, aur ENTRY_CONFLICT 'tumne try kiya, kaam bhi kiya, lekin koi dusra tumse pehle jeet gaya' hai. Yehi wajah hai ki VAULT_BUSY vault-wide ek boolean/counter se aata hai, aur ENTRY_CONFLICT per-entry version number se.
why_needed: Interviewer ko granularity ka sense dikhana zaroori hai -- ek hi 'concurrency error' bolna kaafi nahi, do mechanisms clearly distinguish karna chahiye.
real_world_analogy: VAULT_BUSY jaisa ek counter band hai 'maintenance in progress' board laga kar -- tum try hi nahi kar sakte. ENTRY_CONFLICT jaisa dono ne form submit kiya lekin clerk bataata hai 'kisi aur ne pehle yeh form already process kar diya, tumhara reject'.
how_it_works: VAULT_BUSY: claimEntryOp()/changeMasterPassword ka synchronous check, pehle hi reject. ENTRY_CONFLICT: updateEntry ka commit-ke-baad version comparison.
in_this_project: errors.ts mein VAULT_BUSY comment: 'an entry operation and a master-password rotation are claiming the same vault right now'; ENTRY_CONFLICT comment: 'another operation changed this entry first; this one's work was discarded'.
advantages: Caller behavior ka clear signal -- VAULT_BUSY par thoda wait karke retry karna sense banta hai, ENTRY_CONFLICT par latest data re-fetch karke dobara try karna sense banta hai
Dono alag HTTP 409 maante hain lekin library level par semantics clearly alag hain
disadvantages: HTTP layer dono ko 409 hi map karta hai -- caller ko body ka 'code' field padhna hi padega granularity ke liye
common_mistakes: Dono ko ek hi generic 'CONFLICT' bol dena -- interview mein distinction dikhana important hai
Yeh samajhna ki ENTRY_CONFLICT bhi 'pehle hi reject' karta hai -- nahi, uska kaam already ho chuka tha
follow_up_questions: Can a single operation ever get both VAULT_BUSY and ENTRY_CONFLICT?
Why does the HTTP layer map both to 409?
Would an automatic retry be safe for VAULT_BUSY? For ENTRY_CONFLICT?

question: Walk through redeemShare's single-use claim -- why is NO_SHARING_KEY checked and thrown BEFORE the claim, while a decrypt failure or the recipient's own VAULT_BUSY releases the claim AFTER?
answer_hinglish: redeemShare mein order bahut deliberate hai. Pehle share lookup aur uske revoked/already-redeemed checks (yeh grant ke baare mein hi hain, claim se related nahi). Phir 'if (!record.wrappedPrivateKey) throw NO_SHARING_KEY' -- yeh ek PRECONDITION hai: recipient ne abhi tak apna sharing keypair generate hi nahi kiya, toh yeh koi real redemption attempt nahi tha, bas ek caller-side setup mistake thi. Isiliye yeh claim se PEHLE check hota hai -- share.redeemedAt abhi set nahi hota, one-time use burn nahi hota, aur recipient getSharingPublicKey() call karke phir se try kar sakta hai. Uske BAAD line aati hai 'share.redeemedAt = this.clock.now()' -- yeh synchronous claim hai, exact claim-before-await shape jo claimEntryOp use karta hai, ab ek DIFFERENT resource (share grant) ke liye. Claim ke baad try block mein decrypt, openAsRecipient, aur addEntry (jo khud VAULT_BUSY de sakta hai agar recipient ka vault kisi rotation mein busy ho) sab hote hain. Agar yeh koi bhi genuinely fail ho jaaye -- wrong recipient token (DECRYPTION_FAILED) ya recipient's own VAULT_BUSY -- catch block mein 'share.redeemedAt = null' karke claim RELEASE hoti hai, taaki yeh genuinely ek real attempt tha jo fail hua, aur ek legitimate retry apna ek legitimate shot phir pa sake. Yeh exact distinction test/share-revocation.test.ts aur test/sharing-integration.test.ts mein cover hota hai.
why_needed: Yeh is project ka subtlest ordering decision hai -- precondition-vs-genuine-attempt ka distinction interview mein rare hi explicitly discuss hota hai, lekin yahan code mein exact hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek one-time coupon redeem karne ki machine -- agar tumhare paas card reader hi nahi hai (precondition), machine coupon burn nahi karti; lekin agar card reader se try kiya aur card declined hua (genuine attempt), machine coupon ko 'used' mark karti hai lekin phir refund/release kar deti hai taaki ek real retry ho sake.
how_it_works: Order: grant-level checks -> NO_SHARING_KEY (pre-claim) -> synchronous claim (redeemedAt = now) -> try { decrypt + addEntry } catch { release claim; rethrow }.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts::redeemShare comment: 'NO_SHARING_KEY is checked and thrown BEFORE that claim, since it is not a real attempt; a genuine failure AFTER claiming releases it, so a real retry still gets its one legitimate shot.'
advantages: Precondition failure NEVER burns a legitimate single-use grant
Genuine failure after claiming cleanly releases it -- no permanent lockout from a transient VAULT_BUSY
Same claim-before-await shape reused across two completely different resources (entries, shares)
disadvantages: Between claim and catch, if the process crashed mid-way (not a thrown error), the claim could be left permanently set with no release -- acceptable here since everything is in-memory and a restart clears it anyway
common_mistakes: Checking NO_SHARING_KEY AFTER the claim -- would silently burn a legitimate retry's one-time use for a caller-side setup mistake
Forgetting to release the claim in the catch block, which would make a transient VAULT_BUSY on the RECIPIENT's own vault permanently brick that share
follow_up_questions: What test proves the NO_SHARING_KEY check does not consume the claim?
Why can two concurrent redemptions of the same token never both succeed?
What happens if the recipient's addEntry succeeds but then something threw afterward?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Claim-release-on-failure se legitimate retries protected rehte hain, lekin iska matlab hai share grant object ka 'redeemedAt' field do baar set/unset ho sakta hai failed attempts ke dauraan -- thoda extra mutation, lekin simplicity ke liye worth hai kyunki poora grant in-memory, lightweight object hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar addEntry recipient ke vault par VAULT_BUSY de (kyunki recipient khud kisi rotation mein hai), redeemShare ka claim release ho jaata hai aur caller thodi der baad phir try kar sakta hai -- share waste nahi hota sirf isliye kyunki timing bad luck thi.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alag retry queue ya exponential backoff wrapper caller side add kiya ja sakta hai; ya redeemShare khud ek bounded retry loop internally kar sake agar VAULT_BUSY mile (lekin yeh is project ke 'no automatic retry' design choice ke against jaata).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Shares map in-memory hai -- bahut saare pending shares (lakhon) memory consume karenge; production mein yeh ek TTL/expiry ke saath ek real store mein jaana chahiye, aur claim ko ek atomic DB update se replace karna hoga agar multiple instances hain.
advanced.production_improvements: Share grants ko persist karna (abhi restart par sab gayab ho jaate hain), ek expiry timestamp add karna (abhi sirf revoke/single-use se khatam hote hain), aur failed-claim-release ko metrics mein track karna taaki pata chale kitni baar legitimate retries honi padti hain.

question: What happens to a vault's claim (pendingEntryOps or rotating) when a commit times out via withTimeout/AbortSignal, and how does the codebase guarantee the claim is still released?
answer_hinglish: Har mutating operation (addEntry, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey, changeMasterPassword) apna claim ek try/finally ke andar rakhta hai -- claimEntryOp() (ya rotating=true) try block se PEHLE hota hai, aur finally block mein 'record.pendingEntryOps--' (ya 'record.rotating = false') hamesha chalta hai, chahe commit succeed ho, reject ho, ya timeout ho. commit() khud withTimeout((signal) => this.store.persist(snapshot, signal), this.commitTimeoutMs) call karta hai. withTimeout ek AbortController banata hai, setTimeout se commitTimeoutMs ke baad controller.abort() karta hai aur 'timedOut = true' set karta hai. Agar store.persist() samay par resolve nahi hota, abort signal fire hota hai, run(signal) reject hota hai, aur withTimeout ka catch block dekh kar 'timedOut' true hai toh STORE_TIMEOUT throw karta hai. Yeh error commit() se upar addEntry (ya jo bhi caller hai) tak bubble karta hai -- jiske apne try block mein koi catch nahi hai, toh error seedha throw ho jaata hai, LEKIN finally block phir bhi chalta hai (JS guarantee: finally hamesha chalta hai, chahe try se return ho ya throw). Isi finally mein pendingEntryOps-- (ya rotating=false) hota hai -- claim release ho jaati hai, chahe commit ne kabhi response diya ho ya nahi. test/concurrency.test.ts ka 'a store that never responds' test exactly yeh prove karta hai: timeout ke baad bhi ek later, un-raced rotation successfully chal jaati hai -- matlab claim stuck nahi reh gaya.
why_needed: Ek hung dependency poore vault ko permanently wedge na kar sake -- yeh guarantee production reliability ke liye critical hai, aur interview mein yeh prove karna zaroori hai ki yeh guarantee crash-safe-ish hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek key kisi locker ko temporarily reserve karti hai; agar reservation ka system hang ho jaaye, ek timer force se reservation release kar deta hai, taaki locker permanently 'reserved' na reh jaaye kisi ke bhi fayde ke bina.
how_it_works: try { claim; await commit; apply } finally { release claim } -- JS ka finally guarantee ensures release happens regardless of success, rejection, or timeout.
in_this_project: src/timeout.ts::withTimeout mein AbortController + setTimeout + timedOut flag; src/manager.ts ke har mutating method mein claim-try-finally shape.
advantages: Ek hung store call poore vault ko permanently wedge nahi kar sakta -- claim guaranteed release hoti hai
clearTimeout() finally mein hone se successful commits par timer leak nahi hota (W3 mutation isi ko catch karta hai)
withTimeout ek generic reusable idiom hai, 17-parking-lot se mirrored
disadvantages: STORE_TIMEOUT ke baad bhi store ke andar actual write ho sakta hai (abort signal sirf request karta hai, guarantee nahi deta real I/O turant rukega) -- caller ko pata nahi chalta ki write asal mein hui ya nahi
common_mistakes: Claim release ko try block ke END mein likhna instead of finally -- agar beech mein throw ho, release skip ho jaata
clearTimeout() na karna -- leaked timer (jaisa W3 mutation ne dikhaya) jo test ke process ko hanging rakh sakta tha
follow_up_questions: What does STORE_TIMEOUT NOT guarantee about the underlying store's actual state?
Why does withTimeout need its own timedOut flag instead of just checking signal.aborted in the catch?
What was the W3 mutation, and how was it caught?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: try/finally se claim-release guarantee free milti hai, bina kisi explicit cleanup-on-every-error-path likhe -- lekin iska matlab hai ki agar koi future developer claimEntryOp()/rotating ko try/finally ke bahar likh de, guarantee silently tut jaayegi, aur koi compiler error nahi dega.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar store.persist() abort signal ko ignore kare aur bahut der baad resolve/reject ho (real network client jo signal respect nahi karta), caller ko turant STORE_TIMEOUT mil jaata hai aur claim release ho jaati hai, lekin asal write background mein abhi bhi chal sakta hai -- isse ek 'phantom write' ho sakta hai jo baad mein apply ho jaaye without the caller's knowledge. Yeh project isko explicitly nahi solve karta.
advanced.alternatives: Idempotency key store ke saath bhejna taaki ek late-arriving phantom write safely detect/ignore ho sake; ya store interface ko strictly signal-respecting banane ki requirement rakhna.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Ek slow downstream store par bahut saare concurrent timeouts circuit-breaker jaisa pattern trigger kar sakte hain -- is project mein store ke liye alag circuit breaker nahi hai (sirf breach-check ke liye hai); scale par ek similar breaker store calls ke liye bhi chahiye hoga.
advanced.production_improvements: Store timeout events ko metrics/alerting mein bhejna, STORE_TIMEOUT ke baad reconciliation job jo confirm kare write actually hui ya nahi, aur store interface ko AbortSignal ko mandatorily respect karne ke liye contract test dena.

question: Two changeMasterPassword calls on the same vault run concurrently. Walk through why the second one gets VAULT_BUSY, and why 'rotating' is a boolean rather than a counter like pendingEntryOps.
answer_hinglish: Jab pehla changeMasterPassword call hota hai, woh synchronously verifyMasterPassword karta hai, phir checks karta hai 'if (record.rotating) throw' (abhi false hai, pass) aur 'if (record.pendingEntryOps > 0) throw' (abhi 0 hai, pass), phir 'record.rotating = true' set karta hai -- yeh sab synchronous hai, pehle await (commit) tak koi gap nahi. Jab dusra changeMasterPassword call hota hai (chahe ek hi tick mein ya thodi der baad, jab tak pehla abhi commit ka await kar raha hai), woh bhi apna 'if (record.rotating) throw VAULT_BUSY' check karta hai -- aur ab rotating true hai, toh yeh turant reject ho jaata hai, apna koi commit kabhi try nahi karta. test/concurrency.test.ts ka 'two concurrent master-password rotations' test yahi dikhaata hai: store.pending mein sirf 1 commit hota hai (pehle wale ka), dusra kabhi store tak pahunchta hi nahi. rotating ek boolean hai, counter nahi, kyunki logically sirf EK rotation ek time par meaningful hota hai -- do rotations ko ek saath chalne dena hi galat hoga (kaun sa naya password final hoga), jabki do ADD operations ek saath chalna bilkul theek hai (independent entries, ya version check se safe). Isliye pendingEntryOps ek COUNT hai (kitne parallel entry-ops chal rahe hain, sab allowed), lekin rotating sirf ek on/off flag hai (dusra rotation allowed hi nahi hai jab tak pehla khatam na ho).
why_needed: Yeh dikhaata hai ki concurrency primitives ka SHAPE (boolean vs counter) bhi deliberate design decision hai, random nahi -- usse underlying semantics ka samajh dikhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank account ka PIN change -- ek time par sirf ek PIN-change request process honi chahiye (dusra request turant reject), lekin ek saath kayi ATM withdrawal transactions chal sakti hain (jab tak balance check safe rahe).
how_it_works: rotating: boolean flag, set true synchronously before any await, checked by claimEntryOp() and by changeMasterPassword's own next call. pendingEntryOps: integer, incremented/decremented, allows multiple concurrent entry ops.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts mein VaultRecord interface comment: 'rotating ... true while a changeMasterPassword commit is in flight -- excludes entry ops' vs 'pendingEntryOps ... count of in-flight add/update/delete commits -- excludes rotation'.
advantages: Dusra rotation attempt bina kisi partial work ke turant reject hota hai
Semantics clear hai: rotation ek exclusive operation hai, entry-ops concurrent-safe hain
disadvantages: Agar user genuinely dusri baar password change karna chahta hai jaldi jaldi (retry), unko manually wait karna padta hai pehli rotation khatam hone tak
common_mistakes: rotating ko counter banana -- unnecessarily complex jab boolean kaafi hai
pendingEntryOps ko boolean banana -- isse do legitimate concurrent adds bhi ek doosre ko block kar dete
follow_up_questions: Could two changeMasterPassword calls with the SAME new password both be allowed to proceed safely?
What would change if rotating were a counter instead?
Which wins if the second rotation call arrives a tick later, after the first already completed?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Boolean rotating ek clean 'only one at a time' semantics deta hai, lekin ek downside hai: agar legitimate caller apna password change retry karna chahta hai (maybe network blip se unsure tha ki pehla gaya ya nahi), unhe VAULT_BUSY milta hai jab tak pehla khatam nahi hota -- kabhi kabhi confusing UX, lekin correctness ke liye zaroori.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar rotation ka commit STORE_TIMEOUT de, rotating finally mein false ho jaata hai, toh dusra rotation attempt turant chal sakta hai -- lekin pehle attempt ka actual store-side state ambiguous reh sakta hai (timeout ka matlab reject nahi, bas no-response-in-time).
advanced.alternatives: Queue-based approach jahan dusra rotation request wait kare (block) instead of turant reject -- lekin yeh is project ke 'an error means nothing happened, no implicit waiting' philosophy se match nahi karta.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Single vault ke liye rotation frequency generally low hai (users roz password nahi badalte), toh yeh contention practically rare hai; scale 100x par bhi per-vault rotation rate same rehta hai, horizontal scaling ka asar nahi.
advanced.production_improvements: Caller ko ek clear retry-after hint dena (kitni der mein rotation complete hoga estimate), aur rotation duration ko metrics mein track karna taaki pata chale kitni der tak vault 'busy' rehta hai real workloads mein.

question: The claim-before-await exclusion in this project works because JavaScript cannot preempt synchronous code inside ONE process. What breaks if PasswordManager were horizontally scaled across multiple instances, and how would you redesign the exclusion?
answer_hinglish: rotating aur pendingEntryOps dono in-memory fields hain, ek single process ke VaultRecord object par. Yeh guarantee 'JS synchronous code preempt nahi hota' sirf EK process ke andar true hai. Agar PasswordManager ko horizontally scale kiya jaaye (multiple Node instances, load balancer ke peeche), toh har instance ka apna khud ka VaultRecord in-memory copy hoga -- do instances ek hi ownerId ke liye addEntry aur changeMasterPassword ek saath process kar sakte hain, aur dono apna LOCAL rotating=false dekhenge, kyunki unka apna-apna memory hai. Guarantee poori tarah tut jaati hai, exact wahi bug wapas aa jaata hai jo PLAN.md describe karta hai. Fix karne ke liye do options hain: (1) STICKY ROUTING -- ek consistent-hashing ya ownerId-based sharding layer jo guarantee de ki ek hi ownerId ke saare requests hamesha SAME instance par jaayen, taaki in-memory claim phir se single-process-correct ho jaaye. (2) SHARED/DISTRIBUTED STATE -- rotating/pendingEntryOps ko ek shared store (Redis, ya VaultStore ke andar hi ek locks table) mein move karna, aur claimEntryOp() ko ek atomic operation banana (Redis SETNX+TTL, ya DB mein ek compare-and-swap UPDATE jiska affected-rows count batata hai jeeta ki haara). Yeh dusra approach already ek pattern use kar raha hai jo project mein already exist karta hai -- StoredEntry.version jaisa optimistic concurrency, bas ab vault-level claim ke liye bhi. SESSION_INVALIDATED ka 'generation' counter already distributed-friendly hai, kyunki har session apna captured generation carry karta hai aur comparison lazy, local read hai -- yeh pattern 100x scale par bhi bina shared lock ke kaam karta rahega agar generation khud ek durable, consistently-read field ho.
why_needed: Senior-level interview mein yeh dikhana zaroori hai ki ek elegant single-process trick (synchronous claim) distributed deployment mein automatically nahi scale karta, aur kaun se primitives (DB optimistic lock, sharding) usko replace karte hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti dukaan mein ek hi counter clerk sab customers ek line mein handle karta hai -- fair aur simple. Ab 10 branches khul jaayein bina kisi central inventory system ke -- har branch apna local stock count rakhta hai, aur do branches ek hi item ko 'available' maan kar bech sakte hain jab asal mein ek hi piece bacha tha.
how_it_works: Single-process: in-memory boolean/counter check, synchronous. Distributed: either route by ownerId to one owning instance, or move the claim into a shared, atomically-updatable store (compare-and-swap).
in_this_project: README.md aur PLAN.md dono explicitly likhte hain 'Everything is in memory, one process' aur 'no automatic retry' -- yeh single-process assumption already documented limitation hai, is project ke scope se bahar.
advantages: Sharding by ownerId simplest hai aur existing code ko bilkul change nahi karta
DB-based optimistic lock approach already is project ke version-number pattern se consistent hai, naya concept nahi
disadvantages: Sharding instance failure/rebalancing ke time complex ho jaata hai (jab tak consistent hashing + replication na ho)
Shared-state approach har claim/release ke liye ek extra network round trip add karta hai, jo abhi free (in-memory) hai
common_mistakes: Yeh maan lena ki sirf VaultStore ko ek real DB bana dene se concurrency automatically safe ho jaayegi -- claim/release logic bhi distributed-safe banana padta hai, sirf persistence nahi
Session generation check ko bhi in-memory rakhna jab vault records khud distributed store mein chale gaye ho -- consistency mismatch ho sakta hai
follow_up_questions: Would a Redis-based distributed lock introduce its own new failure modes, like lock expiry during a slow commit?
How would you test this distributed version the way test/concurrency.test.ts tests the in-process one?
Does sharding by ownerId change anything about the sharing feature, which involves TWO independent vaults?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Sticky routing (sharding) rakhta hai existing in-memory claim logic 100% as-is, bas deployment layer change hota hai -- lowest code risk. Shared-state/distributed-lock approach zyada flexible hai (koi bhi instance kisi bhi request ko serve kar sakta hai) lekin naya failure surface (lock expiry, network partition) laata hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Sharding mein agar ek instance crash ho jaaye jiske paas kisi vault ka 'rotating=true' state tha, naya instance jo us ownerId ko lega usko pata hi nahi chalega ki rotation chal rahi thi -- in-memory state poora gaya. Isliye distributed deployment mein yeh claim bhi durable/persisted hona chahiye, pure in-memory nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Database-level advisory locks (jaise Postgres ka advisory lock keyed by ownerId), ya ek dedicated coordination service (Zookeeper/etcd) -- overkill is scale ke liye lekin standard distributed-systems answer.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x par sharding already kaam karta hai bina kisi badlav ke. 100x par hot-owner (ek bahut active ownerId) ek single shard ko bottleneck bana sakta hai -- tab finer-grained per-entry locking (jo already version numbers se partially hai) zyada important ho jaata hai.
advanced.production_improvements: VaultStore ko ek real transactional DB banana aur claim ko compare-and-swap column se replace karna, sharding layer add karna, aur chaos-testing karna (instance kill karke dekhna claim state kya hota hai).

question: Why does this project never store the master password -- not even as a separate hash -- and what is the 'canary' that verifies it instead?
answer_hinglish: Master password khud kahin bhi store nahi hota, hashed bhi nahi. createVault sirf do cheezein banata hai: ek random salt, aur ek 'canary' -- ek FIXED, known plaintext ko real master password se derive ki hui key se AES-256-GCM se encrypt karke. Jab koi unlock() karta hai, candidate password se candidate key derive hoti hai (deriveKey, scrypt ke through), aur phir us key se canary ko decrypt karne ki koshish hoti hai. AES-GCM authenticated encryption hai -- iska authentication tag verify karta hai ki key sahi thi ya nahi; galat key se decrypt() seedha throw karega (authTag match nahi karega), sahi key se woh wapas original plaintext hi decrypt karega. Yehi ek decrypt attempt poora verification mechanism hai -- koi alag 'password hash' field nahi hai jo kabhi salt/key se out-of-sync ho sake. Ek KDF (scrypt), ek artifact (canary) -- do secrets ko sync mein rakhne ka risk hi khatam.
why_needed: Password hash store karna khud ek attack surface hota hai (hash crack ho sakta hai offline). Canary approach se password ka koi bhi derived artifact store nahi hota jo directly password guess karne mein use ho -- sirf ek ciphertext hai jiska content already known hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek locker ka password check karne ka tareeka: ek fixed test item locker ke andar rakha hai; jo chabi use karoge, agar woh sahi khulti hai aur test item mil jaata hai, matlab chabi sahi thi. Locker kahin alag se tumhara password note nahi karta.
how_it_works: createVault: canary = encrypt(deriveKey(password, salt), FIXED_PLAINTEXT). unlock: candidateKey = deriveKey(candidate, salt); decrypt(candidateKey, canary) -- success/throw hi pass/fail hai.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts mein CANARY_PLAINTEXT = Buffer.from('password-manager-canary-v1'); verifyMasterPassword() try/catch ke andar decrypt(candidateKey, record.canary) karta hai -- catch block mein failedAttempts++ aur lockout logic.
advantages: Koi separate hash field nahi, toh drift/sync bug possible hi nahi
AES-GCM ka auth tag already ek free, strong verification signal deta hai
Password cracking ke liye attacker ko bhi scrypt ka poora cost pay karna padta hai, har guess ke liye
disadvantages: Agar koi future developer canary plaintext ko hardcode se change kare bina migration plan ke, purane vaults unreadable ho jaayenge
Canary khud thoda extra storage hai (ek chhota EncryptedBlob) har vault ke liye
common_mistakes: Password ka ek separate SHA-256 hash bhi store karna 'extra safety' ke liye -- yeh do secrets ko sync rakhne ka naya risk banata hai, aur offline-crackable hash hai
Verification ko ek plain string comparison samajh lena -- yeh asal mein ek decrypt-and-check-authTag hai
follow_up_questions: What happens if an attacker gets the canary ciphertext and the salt -- can they verify a guessed password offline?
Why is scrypt chosen over a fast hash like SHA-256 for deriveKey?
What would go wrong if two different vaults used the same fixed canary plaintext but the SAME salt?

question: Explain the k-anonymity protocol isPasswordBreached uses -- exactly what crosses out of the vault, and how does test/breach.test.ts's spy-provider test PROVE that?
answer_hinglish: isPasswordBreached ek real protocol follow karta hai -- wahi jo Have I Been Pwned ka password API use karta hai. Password ka poora SHA-1 hash (sha1Hex) local mein compute hota hai, 40 hex characters ka. Us hash ke sirf pehle 5 characters ('prefix') hi provider.lookupPrefix() ko bheje jaate hain. Provider us prefix se match karne waale saare known-breached password hashes ke SUFFIX (baaki 35 characters) return karta hai. Comparison -- 'suffixes.includes(suffix)' -- LOCALLY hota hai, isi function ke andar; poora hash ya password kabhi bahar nahi jaata. Yeh test/breach.test.ts ke 'never sends more than a 5-character prefix' test mein explicitly proven hota hai: ek spy provider banaya jaata hai jo apne lookupPrefix() call mein jo bhi prefix mila use seen array mein push karta hai. Call ke baad assertions check karte hain: seen.length === 1 (sirf ek call), seen[0].length === 5 (exactly 5 characters), seen[0] password ko contain nahi karta, seen[0] poora hash (sha1Hex(password)) nahi hai, aur sha1Hex(password).startsWith(seen[0]) true hai (matlab yeh genuinely us hash ka prefix hai, random string nahi). Yeh test implementation ko force karta hai ki kabhi bhi accidentally full hash ya password leak na ho.
why_needed: Breach-check service ko password bhejna khud ek privacy risk hai (service provider ya network sniffer tumhara password dekh sakta). K-anonymity isko fix karta hai -- provider itna kam info paata hai ki woh thousands of possible passwords ke saath anonymous rehta hai.
real_world_analogy: Kisi doctor se apni poori medical history batane ke bajaye sirf ek symptom category code bataana, jisse woh ek list of possible conditions de de, aur tum khud apni asli condition match karo -- doctor ko pata hi nahi chalta tumhari exact situation.
how_it_works: sha1Hex -> 40-char hash. prefix = first 5 chars (goes OUT). suffix = remaining 35 chars (stays LOCAL). provider returns all suffixes for that prefix; local includes() check decides true/false.
in_this_project: src/breach.ts::isPasswordBreached comment: 'The only function that ever sees the plaintext password. Only prefix (5 characters) crosses into provider.lookupPrefix'. FakeBreachProvider implements the same contract with a small fixed dataset.
advantages: Password ya poora hash kabhi network/service ko nahi jaata
Ek hi prefix thousands of real-world breached passwords se match ho sakta hai, toh anonymity set bada hai
FakeBreachProvider real protocol shape follow karta hai, toh real HIBP se swap karna easy hoga
disadvantages: Fixed 5-character prefix matlab average suffix-set size predictable hai -- real HIBP mein yeh kaafi bada set hota hai (anonymity ke liye zaroori), is fake dataset mein chhota hai
common_mistakes: Poora hash provider ko bhej dena 'simpler' lagne ke liye
Password ko hash kiye bina hi bhej dena
follow_up_questions: Why SHA-1 specifically, given it is cryptographically broken for collision resistance?
What would happen if the prefix were only 3 characters instead of 5?
How would you cache breach results without storing the plaintext password?

question: Why does keyMatches in src/http/app.ts hash both the configured API key and the caller's key with SHA-256 before calling timingSafeEqual, instead of comparing the raw strings?
answer_hinglish: keyMatches function 'Authorization: Bearer key' header se key nikaalta hai, aur 'timingSafeEqual(expected, digest(match[1]))' karta hai, jahan 'digest' SHA-256 hash leta hai. Do reasons hain yeh hashing step ke liye. Pehla, seedha string comparison ya naive character-by-character loop TIMING LEAK karta hai -- strict equality short-circuit karta hai pehle mismatch par, toh ek attacker response time measure karke dheere dheere pata laga sakta hai ki kitne characters match hue, aur eventually poori key guess kar sakta hai. timingSafeEqual() yeh guarantee deta hai ki comparison ka time sirf buffer LENGTH par depend kare, content par nahi. Dusra, aur subtle reason -- timingSafeEqual DO BUFFERS ki same length maangta hai, warna woh THROW karta hai. Agar expected API key aur caller ki bheji hui key ki length alag ho (jo normal hai -- attacker koi bhi length bhej sakta hai), direct comparison ya toh crash karega ya LENGTH khud ek signal ban jaayega. SHA-256 digest() dono ko HAMESHA exactly 32 bytes mein convert kar deta hai, chahe original key kitni bhi length ki ho -- toh length ka koi bhi leak bhi khatam ho jaata hai, aur timingSafeEqual bina kisi length-mismatch crash ke safely chal sakta hai.
why_needed: Timing-attack ek classic security interview topic hai, aur yeh is project ka ek concrete, code-level example hai jahan constant-time comparison genuinely zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek security guard jo pehle check karta hai badge ka SIZE (fixed hone ki wajah se size hamesha same hai), aur phir ek seal (hash) match karta hai ek hi tarah se, chahe asal badge chhota ho ya bada -- guard ka reaction time kabhi badge ki asli length ya content leak nahi karta.
how_it_works: digest() dono expected key aur caller key ko fixed 32-byte SHA-256 output mein convert karta hai; timingSafeEqual un 32-byte buffers ko constant-time compare karta hai.
in_this_project: src/http/app.ts mein 'const digest = (s: string) => createHash("sha256").update(s).digest();' aur function keyMatches jo match[1] ko digest karke expected se compare karta hai.
advantages: Timing-side-channel pehle se hi band ho jaata hai
Length-mismatch crash bhi avoid ho jaata hai ek hi step mein
digest() ek baar call hone ke liye ekdum cheap hai (SHA-256), auth path slow nahi hota
disadvantages: Agar koi future refactor directly string comparison likh de bina socha-samjha, yeh protection silently chali jaayegi -- koi type-level enforcement nahi hai
common_mistakes: header string ko directly === se Bearer apiKey se compare karna
timingSafeEqual seedha raw strings (different lengths wale) par call karna, jo crash karega
follow_up_questions: What would happen if keyMatches compared lengths before calling timingSafeEqual as a shortcut?
Why hash instead of just padding both strings to the same fixed length?
Is there still any timing signal from the regex match itself?

question: Why does revokeShare throw the IDENTICAL UNKNOWN_SHARE error whether a shareId does not exist at all, or exists but belongs to someone else's vault?
answer_hinglish: revokeShare ka code seedha hai: 'const share = this.shares.get(shareId); if (!share || share.ownerId !== session.ownerId) throw UNKNOWN_SHARE'. Dono conditions -- shareId Map mein hi nahi hai, YA shareId exist karta hai lekin kisi doosre ownerId ka hai -- EK HI error throw karte hain, same code, same message shape. Yeh deliberate hai: agar yeh do cases ko alag error dete, toh ek attacker share-id guessing karke pata laga sakta tha ki ek diya hua shareId KISI bhi vault ne issue kiya tha, chahe woh use revoke na kar paaye. Yeh existence-leak hai -- same class ka problem jaisa 'login failed: wrong password' vs 'login failed: user not found' bolna hota hai, jahan error khud batata hai account exist karta hai ya nahi. Is project mein yahi don't-leak-existence instinct kaafi jagah dohraya gaya hai -- lockout cooldown dono wrong-password aur unknown-user ko same treat karta, aur yahan revokeShare bhi yehi karta hai. test/share-revocation.test.ts explicitly dono cases ko same error ke saath test karta hai, aur confirm karta hai ki bob ka failed revoke attempt (kyunki yeh uska share nahi hai) share ko revoke bhi NAHI karta -- woh abhi bhi valid rehta hai aur redeem ho sakta hai.
why_needed: Security interviews mein 'information leakage via error messages' ek classic topic hai -- yeh is project ka concrete, testable example hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank ke customer care ko koi bolta hai 'mera account number XYZ hai, usko freeze karo' aur account unka nahi hai -- bank bolega 'invalid request', na ki 'yeh account exist karta hai lekin tumhara nahi hai' -- dono cases mein response same rehta hai.
how_it_works: Single boolean-OR condition: '!share || share.ownerId !== session.ownerId' -- ek hi throw statement, ek hi error code, regardless of WHICH condition was true.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts comment: 'Only the vault that issued a share may revoke it... never letting a caller distinguish does not exist from exists but is not yours is the same dont-leak-existence instinct as not telling a login attempt which part was wrong.'
advantages: Attacker ko koi extra information nahi milti shareId guessing se
Ek hi condition, simple aur audit-friendly code
disadvantages: Legitimate caller ko bhi debug karna thoda harder hota hai -- unko pata nahi chalta kya galat tha (typo ya ownership issue)
common_mistakes: Dono cases ke liye alag error codes banana 'better debugging' ke naam par
Error message mein accidentally ownerId ya existence hint include kar dena
follow_up_questions: Where else in this project does the same don't-leak-existence pattern appear?
Should the HTTP layer's logs still distinguish these two cases internally, even if the response does not?
Why is revoking an already-revoked share a no-op instead of an error?

question: Why does changeMasterPassword's old-password check go through the exact same lockout gate (verifyMasterPassword) as unlock(), instead of having its own separate attempt counter?
answer_hinglish: Dono unlock() aur changeMasterPassword() apne andar private verifyMasterPassword(record, candidate) ko call karte hain -- yeh SAME function hai, jo record.failedAttempts aur record.lockedUntil ko read/write karta hai. Agar changeMasterPassword ka apna ALAG counter hota (ya koi counter hi na hota), toh yeh ek 'unrated side door' ban jaata attacker ke liye: unlock() pe lockout lag jaaye, lekin attacker changeMasterPassword endpoint ke through unlimited baar galat oldPassword try kar sakta -- effectively password guessing ka ek DOOSRA rasta, jiska koi rate limit nahi. PLAN.md stage 1 ka decision yahi explicitly kehta hai: 'changeMasterPassword's old-password check goes through the identical lockout gate as unlock() -- otherwise it would be an unrated side door for guessing the password.' Implementation mein yeh automatic hai kyunki dono EK HI function call karte hain, do alag counters maintain karne ki zaroorat hi nahi -- same VaultRecord ke failedAttempts/lockedUntil fields dono entry points se share hote hain. README.md ka test table confirm karta hai: test/change-password.test.ts mein explicitly 'shares the same lockout as unlock()' test hai.
why_needed: Yeh dikhata hai ki ek shared security gate kabhi kabhi 'isolation' se behtar hai -- consistency ensure karna zaroori hota hai jab dono operations ek hi secret guess karne ka attempt hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank jahan ATM PIN attempt counter aur online-banking PIN-verify attempt counter dono EK HI counter share karte hain -- agar alag hote, attacker ek channel use karke doosre channel ka rate limit bypass kar sakta.
how_it_works: unlock() aur changeMasterPassword() dono verifyMasterPassword(record, candidate) call karte hain, jo khud record.failedAttempts/record.lockedUntil update karta hai.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts::verifyMasterPassword comment: 'Shared by unlock() and changeMasterPassword(): both are a prove-you-know-the-master-password check, and both must count against the same lockout.'
advantages: Ek hi code path audit karna hota hai lockout correctness ke liye, do nahi
Attacker ke liye koi 'unrated' guessing endpoint nahi bachta
disadvantages: Agar koi legitimate user frequently password change try kare, unka lockout counter bhi unlock() wale attempts se shared ho jaata hai -- UX thoda confusing ho sakta hai agar woh dono endpoints alternately use karein
common_mistakes: changeMasterPassword ke liye apna khud ka naya failedAttempts field add karna 'isolation' ke naam par
Yeh maan lena ki har endpoint ko apna rate-limit hona chahiye -- kabhi kabhi SHARED gate hi sahi hai
follow_up_questions: What test in test/change-password.test.ts proves this sharing explicitly?
Would it ever make sense for a DIFFERENT operation to have its own separate lockout?
How does lockout interact with multiple sessions already unlocked when the vault gets locked out?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Shared gate se security consistency milti hai minimal code se, lekin UX granularity khoti hai -- ek operation ka lockout doosre operation ko bhi block karta hai, chahe woh bilkul alag use case ho.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi automated script dono unlock() aur changeMasterPassword() ko alternately hit kare galat password se, failedAttempts dono se combine hoke jaldi MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS tak pahunch jaayega -- jo sahi behavior hai, kyunki attacker ka total guess-count hi matter karta hai, kis endpoint se aaya woh nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Per-endpoint rate limiting (HTTP layer par, library se bahar) add karna agar aur granular control chahiye ho, lekin core lockout logic phir bhi shared rehna chahiye correctness ke liye.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Lockout state per-vault hai, toh scale se iska behavior nahi badalta -- ek vault ka lockout doosre vaults ko affect nahi karta. 100x users par bhi per-vault isolation same rehti hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Failed attempts ko bhi ek security-audit log mein bhejna (konsa endpoint se, kab, IP kahan se), aur optionally progressive backoff (har lockout ke baad cooldown badhna) add karna basic fixed cooldown ke upar.

question: Why is RSA-OAEP alone not used to encrypt a whole shared entry, and how does sealForRecipient/openAsRecipient combine it with AES-256-GCM to make this a hybrid (envelope) encryption scheme?
answer_hinglish: RSA asymmetric encryption hai -- bahut slow hai aur sirf ek CHHOTA payload encrypt kar sakta hai (ek 2048-bit RSA key ke saath, OAEP padding ke overhead ke baad, roughly 190 bytes se zyada kuch encrypt nahi ho sakta). Ek entry (title+username+password+notes, JSON serialized) is limit se aasani se bada ho sakta hai, toh RSA se seedha poora entry encrypt karna possible hi nahi hai har case mein, aur jo possible bhi ho woh bahut slow hoga. Isliye sealForRecipient() hybrid/envelope approach use karta hai: pehle ek FRESH, one-time 32-byte AES key banata hai ('const oneTimeKey = randomBytes(32)'), phir entry ka poora plaintext isi AES key se encrypt() karta hai (same AES-256-GCM jo project mein har jagah use hota hai). Phir sirf yeh CHHOTA one-time AES key (32 bytes) RSA-OAEP se recipient ki public key ke saath wrap kiya jaata hai ('publicEncrypt'). Result: ek 'wrappedKey' (RSA se encrypted, chhota) aur ek 'blob' (AES se encrypted, kitna bhi bada ho sakta hai). openAsRecipient() reverse karta hai: pehle wrappedKey ko recipient ki PRIVATE key se unwrap karta hai (privateDecrypt), phir unwrapped AES key se asli blob decrypt karta hai. Yehi exact pattern TLS aur PGP use karte hain -- RSA/asymmetric sirf ek chhoti key exchange ke liye, bulk data ke liye fast symmetric cipher.
why_needed: Hybrid encryption ek standard, well-known pattern hai jo har crypto interview mein pooche jaane ki sambhaavna hai -- isi project ke real code se explain karna strong signal deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek bade parcel ko register post se bhejna slow aur mehenga hota -- isliye tum ek fast courier (AES) se parcel bhejte ho, aur sirf courier ka tracking-id/key ek sealed, trusted envelope (RSA) mein bhejte ho jo sirf recipient khol sakta hai.
how_it_works: sealForRecipient: oneTimeKey = randomBytes(32); blob = encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext); wrappedKey = publicEncrypt(recipientPublicKey, oneTimeKey). openAsRecipient: oneTimeKey = privateDecrypt(recipientPrivateKey, wrappedKey); decrypt(oneTimeKey, blob).
in_this_project: src/sharing.ts comment: 'Asymmetric crypto (RSA-OAEP here) is slow and can only encrypt a small payload, so it is used ONLY to wrap a fresh one-time AES key; the entry's actual content is encrypted with that AES key.'
advantages: Entry size RSA ki size limit se bilkul independent hai
AES encryption/decryption fast hai, RSA sirf ek chhoti key ke liye slow operation karta hai
Same AEAD (AES-256-GCM) poore project mein consistent hai -- ek hi primitive samajhna kaafi hai
disadvantages: Do keys involve hoti hain (one-time AES + RSA keypair), thoda zyada moving parts ek single-key scheme se
RSA keypair generation khud slow hai (roughly 200ms) -- isliye lazily, ek baar per vault generate hota hai
common_mistakes: RSA se directly poora entry encrypt karne ki koshish karna, jo bade payloads par fail ho jaata
Same oneTimeKey ko reuse karna multiple shares ke liye -- har sealForRecipient call apna FRESH key banata hai
follow_up_questions: What is the maximum plaintext size RSA-OAEP alone could encrypt with a 2048-bit key, and why?
Why does a tampered wrappedKey or blob fail with DECRYPTION_FAILED rather than some other error?
What would change if this project used ECIES instead of RSA-OAEP?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: RSA-OAEP ke saath Node ka built-in publicEncrypt/privateDecrypt directly use karna matlab koi extra key-derivation logic likhne ki zaroorat nahi -- lekin RSA keypair generation ek one-time, lazy cost hai jo elliptic-curve-based ECIES se zyada slow hota.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar oneTimeKey generation weak randomness use kare, poora envelope compromise ho sakta hai chahe RSA key kitni bhi strong ho -- isliye randomBytes(32) (crypto-secure) use hota hai, Math.random() nahi.
advanced.alternatives: ECIES (elliptic curve based hybrid encryption) smaller keys aur faster keypair generation deta, lekin apna khud ka key-derivation/KDF logic likhna padta, jo correctness risk badhaata. Project ne RSA-OAEP ko is trade-off mein chuna.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Har share ek naya RSA-OAEP wrap operation hai -- CPU cost fixed per-share hai, scale se linearly badhta hai. 100x shares par yeh CPU-bound workload ban sakta hai jo horizontal scaling se handle hota hai, koi shared-state bottleneck nahi hai sharing ke is hisse mein.
advanced.production_improvements: Key rotation policy for sharing keypairs (abhi sirf changeMasterPassword re-wrap karta hai, naya keypair generate nahi karta), aur bade RSA keys (3072-bit) consider karna long-term security margin ke liye.

question: Why must a breach check NEVER be able to block a password save, and how do the circuit breaker and timeout inside BreachChecker.check() guarantee that it never throws?
answer_hinglish: Is project ka general rule hai 'an error means nothing happened' -- lekin breach-checking ke liye yeh rule DELIBERATELY ulta kiya gaya hai. Breach-check ek NON-CRITICAL dependency hai: agar woh service down ho, slow ho, ya kuch bhi fail ho jaaye, user ko apna password SAVE karne se rokna galat hai -- security feature khud ek availability problem nahi banni chahiye. BreachChecker.check() isi guarantee ko implement karta hai: try block mein breaker.run(withTimeout(...)) call karta hai, aur catch block mein 'return null' karta hai -- yeh method KABHI throw nahi karta, chahe provider error de, chahe timeout ho jaaye, chahe circuit breaker OPEN ho (jo matlab fn() ko call hi nahi kiya jaata). Teeno cases null return karte hain, jiska matlab hai 'breached: unknown', aur addEntry/updateEntry phir bhi successfully save ho jaate hain breached=null ke saath. Timeout ek per-call deadline deta hai taaki ek slow provider har save ko forever hold na kare. Circuit breaker isse ek level upar protect karta hai: agar provider consistently fail kar raha hai, breaker OPEN ho jaata hai aur agle calls provider ko call hi nahi karte (fail-fast), jab tak cooldownMs baad ek half-open trial na ho. Dono mechanisms combine ho kar ensure karte hain ki ek flaky third-party dependency kabhi bhi core password-save functionality ko block na kare.
why_needed: Yeh is project ka sabse deliberately counter-intuitive design decision hai -- 'error means nothing happened' rule ko explicitly todna, aur WHY yeh sahi hai, interview mein strong signal deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek doctor jo patient ki file save karne se pehle background check karna chahta hai, lekin background-check service down hai -- doctor phir bhi patient ka record save kar leta hai 'pending verification' tag ke saath, patient ka treatment rokta nahi.
how_it_works: check() ka try/catch guarantee: provider error, timeout, YA open circuit teeno catch mein pakde jaate hain aur null return hota hai, kabhi exception propagate nahi hoti.
in_this_project: src/breach-checker.ts::BreachChecker.check() mein try { return await this.breaker.run(...) } catch { return null; } -- comment: 'a breach check can NEVER block a save -- the opposite instinct from this project's usual error-means-nothing-happened rule, deliberately.'
advantages: Save path kabhi breach-check service ki health par depend nahi karta
Circuit breaker se repeated timeouts ka cumulative cost bhi bach jaata hai (fail-fast after threshold)
Caller ko honestly 'unknown' signal milta hai, false true/false nahi
disadvantages: Agar provider consistently down rahe, user kabhi bhi apne password ka real breach status nahi jaan payega (hamesha null)
Half-open trial ek failure dekhte hi phir se OPEN ho jaata hai -- recovery thoda conservative hai
common_mistakes: Breach-check fail hone par save ko bhi reject kar dena -- is project ke explicit anti-pattern se ulta
Timeout na lagaana aur ek slow provider ko save ko indefinitely hold karne dena
follow_up_questions: What does the circuit breaker's half-open state actually test, and what happens if that trial also fails?
Why does updateEntry only re-check breach status when the password field actually changed?
What was the BK4 mutation about the default timeout, and how was it caught?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Degrade-to-null approach simplicity deta hai (caller ko sirf true/false/null handle karna hai), lekin iska matlab hai ki security feature silently 'off' ho sakta hai bina kisi loud alert ke agar provider lambe time tak down rahe.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar breach-check provider PERMANENTLY down ho jaaye, breaker hamesha OPEN rahega aur HAR save 'breached: null' degrade karega -- feature silently useless ho jaata hai bina kisi error ke jo kisi ko alert kare, jab tak monitoring circuit state track na kare.
advanced.alternatives: Ek degraded-mode banner/metric expose karna jab circuit lambe samay se open ho, taaki operators ko pata chale security feature effectively off hai; ya ek background health-check job jo independently provider ki status monitor kare.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Per-save ek provider call hota hai -- 100x traffic par provider par load bhi 100x badhta hai, jo real provider ke rate limits se clash kar sakta hai. Caching is scale par zaroori ho jaata hai.
advanced.production_improvements: BreachChecker.getCircuitState() ko metrics/dashboard mein expose karna, prefix-level caching add karna, aur alerting jab circuit lambe samay tak open rahe.

question: How does AES-256-GCM's authentication tag let decrypt() detect a wrong key or tampered ciphertext, and why does the project not need a separate HMAC or signature for this?
answer_hinglish: AES-GCM ek AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) mode hai -- iska matlab hai encryption aur authentication EK HI primitive mein combined hain. encrypt() function cipher.getAuthTag() se ek authTag generate karta hai jo ciphertext (aur implicitly key+IV) par depend karta hai. decrypt() function pehle decipher.setAuthTag(authTag) karta hai, phir decipher.final() call karta hai -- yeh final() call hi authTag verify karta hai internally. Agar key galat ho, YA ciphertext/authTag/IV mein se kuch bhi tamper hua ho, final() EK EXCEPTION throw karta hai -- GCM yeh nahi batata KYUN fail hua (wrong key vs tampered data), sirf batata hai FAIL hua. decrypt() isi exception ko catch karta hai aur DECRYPTION_FAILED throw karta hai. Yeh property hi manager.ts ki poori master-password verification ka base hai (canary decrypt) aur har entry ki integrity ka bhi. Separate HMAC ki zaroorat NAHI hai kyunki GCM ka authTag already ek Message Authentication Code hai, jo khud cipher operation ke saath generate hota hai -- ek alag HMAC layer add karna duplicate/redundant hota aur extra complexity (aur bug-surface) laata bina koi real security benefit ke. test/crypto.test.ts explicitly test karta hai: wrong key, tampered ciphertext, tampered authTag, aur tampered IV -- sab authentication failure, same DECRYPTION_FAILED.
why_needed: AEAD vs encrypt-then-MAC ka difference samajhna crypto-focused interviews mein common follow-up hai, aur yeh is project ka concrete, tested example hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek tamper-evident seal jo khud box ke upar lagaya gaya hai -- seal poora hai toh content genuine hai, seal toota ya mismatch hai toh content ya seal dono ek saath invalid maane jaate hain, koi alag inspection step ki zaroorat nahi.
how_it_works: encrypt: cipher.getAuthTag() ciphertext + key + IV se derive hota hai. decrypt: setAuthTag() + final() internally verify karta hai; mismatch par exception.
in_this_project: src/crypto.ts::decrypt mein try/catch ke andar decipher.final() call, catch block mein 'ciphertext failed authentication (wrong key or tampered data)' DECRYPTION_FAILED throw hota hai.
advantages: Encryption aur integrity-check ek hi primitive mein -- kam moving parts
Har master-password check (canary) aur har entry read effectively tamper-detection bhi deta hai free mein
Well-audited standard algorithm, Node built-in
disadvantages: GCM IV REUSE ke liye catastrophically fragile hai -- ek hi key ke saath IV reuse hua toh authentication aur confidentiality dono poori tarah broken ho jaate hain, isliye encrypt() har call par fresh randomBytes(IV_LENGTH) banata hai
common_mistakes: GCM ke upar bhi apna khud ka HMAC layer add karna 'extra safety' -- redundant aur over-engineering
IV ko fixed ya predictable rakhna 'simplicity' ke liye -- yeh poora scheme break kar deta hai
follow_up_questions: What specifically breaks if the same IV is reused twice under the same key?
Why can decrypt() not distinguish a wrong key from tampered ciphertext, and does that matter?
What were the K1/K2/K3 mutations in crypto.ts, and what did each one break?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: AEAD se separate signing/HMAC layer ki zaroorat khatam ho jaati hai, simplicity milti hai -- lekin iska matlab hai poora security model ek hi primitive (AES-GCM) ki correctness par depend karta hai; IV management ek single point of failure ban jaata hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar randomBytes() kabhi weak/predictable IV de, authentication guarantee compromise ho sakta hai. Mutation K2 (encrypt reuses a fixed IV) explicitly test karta hai ki IV reuse hi na ho.
advanced.alternatives: AES-256-CBC + separate HMAC-SHA256 (encrypt-then-MAC) ek purana alternative hai, jo manually implement karna padta aur order-of-operations bugs ka risk hota. GCM yeh sab eliminate karta hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Encryption/decryption per-operation cost scale ke saath linearly badhta hai, lekin AES-NI hardware acceleration ke saath yeh negligible hai even at high throughput -- scale par koi naya crypto design change ki zaroorat nahi.
advanced.production_improvements: Key rotation ke liye ek versioned encryption scheme (algorithm version field blob mein) add karna future-proofing ke liye, aur periodic re-encryption audits.

question: If FakeBreachProvider were replaced with a real network call (like the real Have I Been Pwned password API), what would change in BreachChecker's design at 10x-100x traffic, and what new failure modes would appear?
answer_hinglish: Abhi FakeBreachProvider ek in-memory, instant-response dataset hai -- koi real network latency, rate limiting, ya DNS/TLS overhead nahi. Real HIBP API call karne par kayi naye concerns aayenge. Pehla, NETWORK LATENCY aur VARIABILITY -- real call mein 50ms se 2000ms+ tak latency ho sakti hai, aur DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS ko real-world p99 latency ke against tune karna padega, warna bahut saare legitimate calls timeout honge. Dusra, THIRD-PARTY RATE LIMITS -- HIBP apna khud ka rate limit lagata hai per API key; 100x traffic par agar har addEntry/updateEntry apna breach-check call kare, yeh rate limit se clash karega, aur circuit breaker constantly OPEN reh sakta hai sirf rate-limiting ki wajah se, provider genuinely down na hone par bhi. Teesra, CACHING zaroori ho jaata hai -- same 5-character prefix baar baar query karna wasteful hai; ek short-TTL cache network calls drastically kam kar sakta hai, kyunki breached-password dataset slowly hi change hota hai. Chautha, COST -- real APIs free-tier limits ya paid-tier costs laate hain, jo per-call cost ko ek business metric bana dete hain, na sirf latency metric. Circuit breaker aur timeout already yahan foundational hain, lekin production mein unhe CACHING LAYER ke saath combine karna zaroori hoga, aur circuit state ko observability mein expose karna hoga taaki ek silently-degraded security feature khud ek incident na ban jaaye.
why_needed: Senior-level interview mein 'yeh fake hai, production mein real hota toh kya badalta' ek standard follow-up hai -- honest answer dena zaroori hai ki kya already handled hai aur kya naya hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti dukaan apne khud ke stock se order fulfill karti hai (fake provider, instant) -- jab woh ek bahut bade supplier (real HIBP) se order lena shuru karti hai, suddenly shipping delays, order limits, aur cost-per-order sab naye factors ban jaate hain jo pehle exist hi nahi karte the.
how_it_works: Same BreachChecker interface (provider/breaker/timeout) rehta hai -- sirf BreachProvider implementation badalta hai FakeBreachProvider se ek real HTTP-calling provider mein.
in_this_project: README.md explicitly kehta hai: 'FakeBreachProvider is a small, fixed, explicitly-fake in-memory dataset -- not a real breach database, and not a real network call. The k-anonymity protocol it speaks is real.' Yeh is project ki honest, documented limitation hai.
advantages: BreachProvider interface already abstraction provide karta hai -- sirf implementation swap karni hai, BreachChecker/CircuitBreaker/timeout logic bilkul same rehta hai
Circuit breaker aur timeout already production-grade resilience patterns hain jo real network call ke liye bhi directly kaam karenge
disadvantages: Abhi koi caching layer nahi hai -- real deployment mein zaroori ban jaayega
Rate-limit-caused failures aur genuine-outage failures circuit breaker ke liye currently distinguish nahi hote -- dono 'failure' hi maane jaate hain
common_mistakes: Yeh maan lena ki sirf provider swap kar dene se production-ready ho jaayega -- caching, rate-limit-awareness, aur observability bhi chahiye
Timeout value ko fake provider ke zero-latency assumption par based rakhna
follow_up_questions: How would you design the cache key and TTL for prefix-level breach results?
Should rate-limit responses from a real provider be treated differently from other errors by the circuit breaker?
What observability would you add to detect a silently-degraded (always-null) breach check in production?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: BreachProvider interface ki clean abstraction se swap easy hai, lekin resilience primitives (timeout, breaker) jo fake provider ke liye already 'enough' lagte hain, real provider ke actual latency/rate-limit profile ke against RE-TUNE karne padenge.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Real provider ka rate-limit response agar generic error jaisa treat ho, circuit breaker usko 'provider down' samajh kar OPEN ho jaayega, jabki asal mein provider healthy hai, sirf throttling kar raha hai -- is distinction ko handle karna production mein zaroori hai.
advanced.alternatives: Ek local, periodically-refreshed bloom filter / dataset of breached password hashes (jaisa kuch real-world password managers karte hain) network dependency poori tarah eliminate kar sakta hai, cost of storage ke against.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x traffic par caching ke bina provider load linearly badhta hai aur rate limits se clash hone ka risk badhta hai; caching ke saath cache-hit-ratio high hone par load sublinear ho sakta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Prefix-level caching with TTL, rate-limit-aware circuit breaker, metrics dashboard for circuit state aur breach-check latency, aur fallback to a local dataset jab remote provider lambe time degraded rahe.

question: Walk through this project's overall security model end to end -- what threats does it actually defend against, and what does README.md's 'Known and NOT handled' section explicitly admit it does NOT cover?
answer_hinglish: Poora security model layer-by-layer dekhte hain. (1) Master password KABHI stored nahi, canary+AES-GCM se verify hota hai -- offline password-database-theft se bhi master password directly recover nahi hota, scrypt ki wajah se brute-force bhi expensive hai. (2) Repeated wrong attempts LOCKOUT trigger karte hain (shared gate unlock() aur changeMasterPassword ke beech) -- online guessing slow ho jaati hai. (3) Har entry AES-256-GCM se encrypted hai at rest -- VaultStore mein ya exportVault mein kabhi plaintext nahi dikhta. (4) Breach-checking k-anonymity se karta hai -- kabhi password ya poora hash leak nahi hota provider ko. (5) Sharing hybrid/envelope encryption se hota hai -- do independent vaults ek doosre ki master password/key/private-key kabhi nahi dekhte. (6) Shares single-use aur revocable hain, claim-before-await se race-safe. (7) revokeShare don't-leak-existence follow karta hai. (8) HTTP layer constant-time API-key comparison use karta hai. Ab README.md ka 'Known and NOT handled' section honestly kehta hai: sab kuch EK PROCESS mein in-memory hai, restart par sab gaya (shares, sessions sab). Koi 2FA nahi hai. Koi password-strength scoring nahi hai generator ke charset rules se aage. Ek bahut persistent attacker jo MULTIPLE ownerIds ke against try kare, uske liye koi cross-vault rate limiting nahi hai (sirf per-vault lockout hai). HTTP layer mein CORS, per-end-user session/cookie layer, ya apna khud ka rate limiting bhi nahi hai. lock()'s 'discard the key' best-effort hai -- JS mein Buffer memory ko reliably zero karna possible nahi hai. Yeh sab explicitly documented limitations hain, bugs nahi.
why_needed: Senior interview mein 'tumhara system kahan FAIL karega / kya nahi karta' poochna common hai -- honest, specific answer (invented nahi) interviewer ko confidence deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek ghar mein strong locks aur alarm system laga hai (encryption, lockout) lekin ghar waale khud admit karte hain ki unke paas fire sprinkler nahi hai aur neighbourhood watch nahi hai -- woh scope clearly bata dete hain, chhupa kar nahi rakhte.
how_it_works: Har layer apna specific threat address karta hai; README's explicit 'NOT handled' list scope boundary define karta hai taaki koi false sense of completeness na ho.
in_this_project: README.md ka poora 'Known and NOT handled (stage 7)' section -- yeh is project ki sabse honest, interview-ready documentation hai, kyunki yeh scope boundary clearly define karta hai.
advantages: Har threat ka specific, testable defense hai (test files isi ko prove karte hain)
Limitations explicitly documented hain -- koi false confidence nahi
disadvantages: In-memory, single-process design production-grade persistence/availability ke liye insufficient hai
Cross-vault rate limiting ka na hona ek real gap hai agar multi-tenant deployment ho
common_mistakes: Yeh claim karna ki project 2FA support karta hai ya koi aisi feature jo asal mein nahi hai
Limitations ko chhupaana instead of unhe explicitly discuss karna interview mein
follow_up_questions: Which single limitation would you fix FIRST before any production deployment?
How would cross-vault rate limiting be added without touching the per-vault lockout logic?
Why is 'best-effort key discard' acceptable here but might not be in a different context?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Scope ko explicitly chhota rakhna (no 2FA, no persistence, no cross-vault rate limit) is project ko LLD-interview-focused banata hai -- depth over breadth. Production system isi foundation par build karega, lekin kayi naye layers add karne padenge.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Ek persistent attacker jo ek hi IP se 1000 different ownerIds try kare, per-vault lockout har ek vault ko individually lock karega, lekin attacker total requests unlimited rehte hain -- yeh explicitly 'not covered' hai aur ek real DoS/guessing vector hai production mein.
advanced.alternatives: Ek API-gateway-level rate limiter (per-IP ya per-API-key) is project ke bahar add kiya ja sakta hai bina library code touch kiye -- README isi suggestion ko already hint karta hai 'that is a transport/API-layer concern'.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x users par in-memory sessions/shares/vaults map memory-bound ho jaayenge -- real persistence layer zaroori ban jaata hai, aur multi-instance deployment ke liye concurrency primitives redesign chahenge.
advanced.production_improvements: Persistent VaultStore backend, 2FA support, API-gateway rate limiting, security audit logging, aur periodic penetration testing against the documented threat model.

question: Design the end-to-end security of sharing one entry between two independent vaults in this project -- from shareEntry through redeemShare to revokeShare -- and explain what guarantee holds at each step.
answer_hinglish: Poora flow EK chain hai jahan har step apna specific guarantee deta hai. Step 1, getSharingPublicKey: har vault apna RSA keypair LAZILY generate karta hai (sirf first use par), private key vault ki OWN key se encrypted store hota hai -- kabhi clear text mein nahi, chahe vault ki apni storage ke andar bhi. Step 2, shareEntry: sender apna entry decrypt karta hai (apni session key se), phir sealForRecipient() se hybrid-encrypt karta hai recipient ki PUBLIC key ke against -- yeh ek PURE, SYNCHRONOUS operation hai, sender ka vault state bilkul nahi badalta, sirf ek grant manager-wide shares Map mein register hota hai. Step 3, redeemShare: recipient apni PRIVATE key se token unwrap karta hai (openAsRecipient) -- is step mein checks order mein hote hain: pehle UNKNOWN_SHARE/SHARE_REVOKED/SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED (grant ke baare mein), phir NO_SHARING_KEY (precondition, claim se PEHLE), phir claim (redeemedAt = now(), synchronous, single-use guarantee), phir actual decrypt+addEntry (jo FAIL hone par claim release kar deta hai). Step 4, revokeShare: sirf issuing vault revoke kar sakta hai, aur unknown/not-yours dono SAME error dete hain (don't-leak-existence). Guarantees jo hold karte hain: (a) neither vault EVER sees the other's master password, vault key, ya private key -- sirf public key aur sealed token exchange hote hain; (b) share EXACTLY once redeemable hai, concurrent attempts ke against bhi (claim-before-await); (c) ek tampered ya wrong-recipient token DECRYPTION_FAILED deta hai, claim consume NAHI karta; (d) sender ka password rotate hone ke baad bhi sharing kaam karta hai, kyunki private key bhi re-wrap hoti hai changeMasterPassword mein; (e) redeemed entry recipient ke OWN addEntry path se guzarta hai, toh usko recipient ki apni breach-check configuration aur claim/commit exclusion bhi automatically milti hai, koi duplicate logic ke bina.
why_needed: Sharing feature is project ka sabse multi-layered security surface hai -- interviewer ko ek system-design-level, end-to-end walkthrough dikhana sabse strong answer hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek registered, tamper-evident, single-use courier envelope jisko sirf recipient ki chabi khol sakti hai, jiska tracking number sender cancel kar sakta hai jab tak delivered na ho, aur jo delivery ke baad apna khud ka independent record banata hai recipient ke paas, sender se disconnected.
how_it_works: getSharingPublicKey -> shareEntry (seal, register grant) -> redeemShare (unwrap, claim, addEntry) -> revokeShare (ownership-checked, idempotent).
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ke shareEntry/redeemShare/revokeShare methods aur src/sharing.ts ka sealForRecipient/openAsRecipient; README.md ka 'One entry can be shared...' bullet aur PLAN.md ke stage 4/5 decisions.
advantages: Har step ka security property independently testable hai (sharing.test.ts, sharing-integration.test.ts, share-revocation.test.ts)
redeemShare addEntry reuse karta hai -- duplicate claim/commit/breach-check logic ka risk hi nahi
Private key rotation-safe hai -- ek real gap jo explicitly fix kiya gaya
disadvantages: Koi directory service nahi -- public key exchange out-of-band caller ki responsibility hai
Revocation/single-use sirf REDEEM se PEHLE kaam karta hai -- redeem ho jaane ke baad recipient ki copy permanently unki hai, waapas nahi li ja sakti
common_mistakes: NO_SHARING_KEY check ko claim ke BAAD karna -- legitimate retry ka one-time use burn ho jaata
revokeShare mein ownership check skip karna -- koi bhi kisi ka share revoke kar sakta
follow_up_questions: What test proves a wrong-recipient token does not consume the share's single use?
Why does redeemShare call addEntry instead of writing its own insertion logic?
What would it take to support revoking a share AFTER it has been redeemed?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Redeem-reuses-addEntry design se code duplication zero hai, lekin iska matlab hai redeemShare ki latency addEntry ki poori latency (claim+commit+breach-check) inherit karti hai -- ek simple unwrap operation se zyada slow.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar sender apna entry delete kar de SHARE karne ke baad lekin redeem hone se PEHLE, redeem par koi asar nahi padta -- token khud ek self-contained sealed copy hai, sender ke current vault state se independent. Yeh ek deliberate property hai, bug nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Ek 'live reference' sharing model (jahan recipient sender ke entry ko REFERENCE kare, copy nahi) alag trade-offs deta -- real-time sync possible hota lekin sender-recipient coupling badh jaata, aur revocation-after-redeem bhi possible ho jaata (jo abhi explicitly NOT supported hai).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Shares Map in-memory hai -- lakhon pending shares memory-heavy ho sakte hain production mein; ek TTL/expiry add karna zaroori hoga stale grants clean karne ke liye bade scale par.
advanced.production_improvements: Share expiry (time-based, abhi missing), ek directory service for public key exchange, aur redeem-after-revoke-race ko dashboard/metrics mein track karna.
